# Assess alignment between classifications {#sec-alignment}

Conceptual alignment is the first principle for cross-referencing classifications. Units in both the source and target classification should be based on similar concepts. 

Cross-referencing aims to elucidate relationships between units of classifications that represent similar types of entities. To be cross-referenced to the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology (IUCN GET), it follows that the units of the source classification must be aligned with the ecosystem concept. 

Based on the definition agreed upon by @UNCBD_1992, following @Tansley_1935 original concept, an ecosystem is:

> “a dynamic complex of plant, animal and micro-organism communities and their non-living environment interacting as a functional unit”. 

Qualitatively different kinds of entities should not be compared to the IUCN GET. In some cases partial relationships or conceptual overlaps may arise, and these warrant rigorous evaluation in cross-referencing to determine eligibility. For example land use and land cover classes or types are sometimes used as proxies of structural features of ecosystems, but they lack information on compositional and functional features.

## Eligibility of units

Most units in the TASVEG dataset represent vegetation communities and can be considered eligible for crossreferencing to the IUCN GET. 

However, there are three mapping units in the group 'Other natural environments' that require more scrutiny: Lichen lithosere (ORO), Sand, mud (OSM), and Water, sea (OAQ).

According to the technical manual [@KitchenerHarris_2013]:

> Lichen lithosere (ORO) is important for undisturbed cryptogamic communities, such as on blockstreams, cliffs, talus and scree slopes and exposed bedrock on mountain tops and ridges. 

> Sand, mud (OSM) is bare of vegetation, has been used for mapping beaches, sand dune systems, and mobile sand sheets such as those at Waterhouse in north-east Tasmania or at Sandy Cape on the west coast. 

> Water, sea (OAQ) has been used to designate areas of sea, artificial impoundments such as Lake Gordon, Lake Saint Clair and Lake Pedder, as well as deep water in natural lakes.

The units OAQ and OSM are mapping units combining multiple types of ecosystems 

## Lookup tables for both classifications

For the next steps of this workflow we will need lookup tables with the valid units of both classifications. 

For the TASVEG classification we can explore the look up table to display the basic information for each unit.

:::{.aside}

Our setup for this R session is: 

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
here::i_am("preparation/index.qmd")
library(foreign)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ecoSynthesis)
output_dir <- here::here("output-XREFs")
```

:::

```{r}
TASVEG_DBF <-
    read.dbf(here::here("gisdata", "TASVEG_5_0_Fire_Attributes_LUT.dbf"),
        as.is = TRUE
    )
```

We focus on three attributes:

|Attribute Name | Full Name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| VEG_GROUP | Vegetation Group  | The broad vegetation group to which the polygon belongs. This field can be used for  rapid categorisation of polygons for display. |
| VEGCODE | Vegcode | Three letter code that defines the dominant TASVEG vegetation community present within the polygon.| 
|VEGCODE_D | Vegcode Description |The full name of the community described by the VEGCODE attribute. |

```{r}
TASVEG_LUT <-
    TASVEG_DBF |>
    select(VEG_GROUP, VEGCODE, VEGCODE_D) |>
    arrange(VEG_GROUP, VEGCODE) |>
    unique() |>
    as_tibble()
```


```{r}
DT::datatable(TASVEG_LUT)
```

Here we flag the units that are deemed not eligible and convert this table into a `lookup_tbl` object:

```{r}
not_eligible <- c("OAQ", "OSM", "ORO")
TASVEG <- TASVEG_LUT |>
    mutate(eligible = !(VEGCODE %in% not_eligible)) |>
    lookup_tbl("VEGCODE", "VEGCODE_D", "eligible")

TASVEG
```

For the IUCN GET, we use the `IUCN_GET_LUT` data included in the `ecoSynthesis` package and assume all units are eligible and valid:

```{r}
IUCN_GET <- lookup_tbl(IUCN_GET_LUT, "efg_id", "efg_name")
```

:::{.aside}

We save both lookup tables in a file that we can load in later steps of the workflow:

```{r}
save(TASVEG, IUCN_GET, file = here::here(output_dir, "lookup-tables.rda"))
```

:::
